newsitem.title: CUBA: Cuba aims for single currency, doesn't say when.
newsitem.headline: Cuba aims for single currency, doesn't say when.

text.p: Cuban authorities aim for an eventual phasing out of the current system of dual curencies -- the peso and the U.S. dollar, a senior official has said.

Finance Minister Manuel Millares told a conference on accountancy in Havana Tuesday evening that "the aim is to continue to strengthen the national currency so that when the right time comes we can eliminate dual currency".
Millares did not say when this moment might come, but added that improved productivity and efficiency in the economy were crucial to strengthening the peso.

Cuba legalised possession of hard currency in August 1993, and since then the country has effectively had two currencies in use, the peso and the U.S. dollar. Dollars are used to buy products in hard currency stores, originally catering to foreign residents but now open to any Cuban with dollars.

Cubans who have dollars, because they receive remittances from relatives abroad, or because they have jobs with foreign companies or in tourism, are far better off than those earning pesos. But this gap has narrowed with a strengthening of the peso over the last three years, from a low of about 150 pesos to the dollar in mid-1994 to a current 21 pesos to the dollar.

Authorities say the improvement is due to a recovery from the worst of the crisis caused by the collapse of the former Soviet Union and to measures from 1994 onwards to reduce excess peso liquidity, such as price rises on non-essential goods like cigarettes and rum.
